blocks.text: Sodium explodes on contact with water while neon sits inertly inside a shop sign. They are next-door neighbours in the periodic table, yet they behave completely differently. The only difference that matters is one electron, and where it sits.

blocks.markdown:
## Shells and their capacity

Electrons occupy energy levels, or **shells**, numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4 outwards from the nucleus. The maximum number of electrons a shell can hold is $2n^2$.

- Shell 1 (K): 2 electrons
- Shell 2 (L): 8 electrons
- Shell 3 (M): 18 electrons
- Shell 4 (N): 32 electrons

For the first twenty elements the simple shell notation is enough. Calcium, with 20 electrons, is written **2, 8, 8, 2** — the third shell pauses at 8 because the 4s subshell fills before the 3d.

blocks.title: Subshells
blocks.text: Each shell is divided into subshells labelled s, p, d and f. An s subshell holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14. Written in full, the electron configuration of calcium is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2.

items: Aufbau principle: electrons fill the lowest available energy subshell first. The order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p.
Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most two electrons and they must have opposite spins.
Hund's rule: within a subshell, electrons occupy separate orbitals singly with parallel spins before any orbital receives a second electron.

blocks.markdown:
### Reading the periodic table from the configuration

Two rules do almost all the work:

- The **period number** equals the number of occupied shells, that is the largest value of n.
- The **group number** for main-group elements equals the number of electrons in the outermost shell.

So an element with configuration 2, 8, 6 has three shells and six outer electrons: period 3, group VI. That is sulphur.

blocks.title: Placing an element from its atomic number
blocks.prompt: An element has atomic number 15. Write its electron configuration and state its period, group and likely ionic charge.

steps.text: Atomic number 15 means a neutral atom has 15 electrons.
Fill the shells in order: 2 in the first, 8 in the second, leaving 15 - 10 = 5 for the third. Shell notation is 2, 8, 5.
Three shells are occupied, so the element is in period 3.
There are 5 electrons in the outermost shell, so it is in group V.
Needing 3 more electrons to reach the stable octet, it forms a 3- ion. The element is phosphorus, which forms the phosphide ion P3-.

blocks.answer: 2, 8, 5 or 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p3; period 3, group V, forms a 3- ion

blocks.title: Why the noble gases are unreactive
blocks.text: Helium has a full first shell (2) and the other noble gases have eight electrons in the outer shell. A full outer shell is a low-energy, stable arrangement, so these atoms have no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons. Every other atom reacts in order to reach that same arrangement.

blocks.title: The 4s before 3d trap
blocks.text: Because 4s is lower in energy than 3d, potassium is 2, 8, 8, 1 and not 2, 8, 9. Writing 2, 8, 9 is one of the most frequent errors in this topic. Remember: the third shell holds 18 in total, but it only takes the last 10 after 4s has filled.

points: Shell capacity is 2n squared, giving 2, 8, 18 and 32 for the first four shells.
Electrons fill the lowest available subshell first, in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p.
Hund's rule puts one electron in each orbital of a subshell before pairing begins.
Period number equals the number of occupied shells; group number equals the number of outer-shell electrons.
A full outer shell explains the inertness of the noble gases and the charges other elements adopt.
